To "kick yourself" means to feel deep frustration, regret, or anger directed at yourself because you made a mistake, missed an opportunity, or did something foolish that you clearly could have avoided.

It is the feeling of "I should have known better!" or "Why did I do that?!"

Literally, kicking yourself means physically hitting your own body with your foot — which is painful and makes no real sense to do. That's exactly the point. The idiom captures the idea that your regret is so strong, it feels like you want to punish yourself physically. Of course, nobody actually does this — it is purely an expression of intense self-blame.

Think of a time when you did something — or didn't do something — and immediately thought, "That was such an obvious mistake. I knew better. How did I let this happen?"

That sharp, sinking, self-directed frustration? That is exactly what "kick yourself" describes.

It is not just mild disappointment. It is the kind of regret that stings — especially because the mistake or missed chance feels preventable in hindsight.

1. It is always about regret you feel toward yourself.
You don't kick someone else — you kick yourself. The blame, frustration, and disappointment are all pointed inward, at your own actions or decisions.

2. The regret is usually about something avoidable.
The pain of "kicking yourself" is strongest when you realize the mistake was unnecessary. You had the information, the chance, or the ability — but you still got it wrong or let it slip away.

3. It can be about action OR inaction.
You can kick yourself for doing something wrong, and you can kick yourself for failing to do something you should have done.

The idiom is most commonly used in these patterns:

  • "You'll kick yourself" — a warning that someone will regret something
  • "I could kick myself" — expressing current regret
  • "I kicked myself" — describing past regret
  • "He/she kicked himself/herself" — describing someone else's regret

Example 1:

"I could kick myself — I had tickets to that concert but I sold them, and it turned out to be the best show of the year."

→ The person sold their tickets thinking it wasn't a big deal. Later, they realized it was a huge mistake. The regret is strong because they had the opportunity right in their hands and gave it away.

Example 2:

"You'll kick yourself if you don't apply for that job. You're perfectly qualified."

→ Here, someone is warning a friend. They're saying: "If you let this chance go, you are going to deeply regret it later." It's used as a push or motivation.

Example 3:

"She kicked herself for not buying that house when the price was low. Now it costs twice as much."

→ She had the chance to buy at a good price but didn't. Now she has to live with that decision. The regret is sharp because the answer was obvious in hindsight.

Example 4:

"I kicked myself when I realized I had the answer all along but wrote something completely different."

→ The person had the right knowledge but still made the wrong choice. That kind of self-inflicted mistake produces exactly this type of regret.

Example 5:

"Don't let this sale end without buying — you'll kick yourself tomorrow."

→ A warning that inaction (not buying) will lead to strong regret when the opportunity is gone.

You will hear "kick yourself" in everyday spoken English and informal writing. It appears in:

  • Personal conversations — when someone shares their regret with a friend
  • Advice or warnings — to encourage someone not to miss an opportunity
  • Storytelling — when someone describes a past mistake
  • Sales and marketing language — "You'll kick yourself if you miss this deal!"

It is informal in tone. You would use it comfortably with friends, family, and colleagues in casual settings. In a very formal written document (like a legal report or academic paper), you would instead write something like "deeply regret" or "reproach oneself."
The Difference Between "Kick Yourself" and Simple Regret

Normal regret: "I wish I had done that." — mild, calm disappointment.

Kicking yourself: "I CANNOT BELIEVE I didn't do that. I knew better. How could I?!" — sharp, stinging, self-directed frustration.

The idiom carries more emotional intensity than simply saying "I regret it." It suggests the mistake felt avoidable and obvious, which makes the regret hurt more.

"Kick yourself" vs. "Bite your tongue"
These are different. "Bite your tongue" means stopping yourself from saying something. "Kick yourself" is about regretting a past action or decision — it has nothing to do with speech specifically.

"Kick yourself" vs. "Shoot yourself in the foot"
"Shooting yourself in the foot" means accidentally harming your own chances or situation through your own actions. It's similar but focuses more on accidentally sabotaging yourself, while "kick yourself" focuses more on the emotional regret you feel afterward.

The idiom comes from the visual image of someone being so frustrated with themselves that they want to physically kick their own body as a form of self-punishment. Since you truly can't kick yourself effectively (try it — it's nearly impossible!), the phrase emphasizes just how irrational and overwhelming the feeling of self-blame can be. Language borrowed this physical image to express a powerful emotional experience.
